query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an in-situ argon shrouding system around the thermal spray plume during HVOF deposition of the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat will reduce in-flight oxidation and enhance inter-splat bonding, thereby increasing the effective coating thickness compared to the standard 15–45 μm feedstock deposition.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy powder with a particle size range of 15–45 μm used for bond coat deposition.
generation.intervention: Introduce an in-situ argon (or similarly inert gas) shrouding system around the spray plume during the HVOF thermal-spray deposition process.
generation.conditions: Conducted during thermal-spray deposition under standard HVOF parameters and maintained effectiveness during subsequent service in thermal barrier coating systems operating at elevated temperatures (e.g., around 800 °C) with thermal cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduction in the formation of superficial oxide layers on the molten droplets will preserve the alloy’s composition and BCC phase integrity while promoting more effective splat bonding and lower porosity.
generation.mechanism: The argon shroud limits ambient oxygen exposure during the particles’ flight, thereby minimizing in-flight oxidation. This suppression of oxidative reactions retains the powder’s reactive integrity, enhances droplet cohesion upon impact, and promotes greater deposition efficiency and uniform coating growth.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is expected to produce a coating with increased thickness—meeting or exceeding the targeted bond coat dimensions—while maintaining minimal as-sprayed oxidation and high coating integrity compared to the baseline process.
generation.baseline: Bond coats produced from 15–45 μm feedstock under conventional HVOF conditions without any inert gas shrouding, resulting in insufficient thickness and higher oxidation levels.
generation.boundary: The effect is anticipated to hold under standard HVOF operating conditions and typical thermal barrier coating service environments. Effectiveness may depend on optimizing the shroud’s gas flow dynamics; deviations may affect particle heating or momentum transfer.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in thickness and degree of oxidation suppression is uncertain until detailed experimental optimization is performed. Additionally, interactions between the gas shroud and spray plume dynamics may require further tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled study with two sets of deposition runs using identical HVOF parameters. One set will employ the in-situ argon shrouding system, while the control set will use conventional ambient conditions. All other parameters (e.g., feed rate, spray distance, substrate preparation) should be kept constant.
measurements: Oxide content and phase composition (analyzed via XRD and EDS)
Porosity and microstructural quality (assessed by SEM)
Adhesion strength (evaluated using standardized mechanical tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings produced with the argon shrouding system do not show a statistically significant increase in thickness and a measurable reduction in oxidation levels, while maintaining or enhancing adhesion and microstructural integrity relative to the control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). It is known [] that when Al concentration in FeCoNiCrAlMo0.5 is lower than 10%, FCC solid solution becomes preferable to BCC.
